result: Spatial attention is fully available at the task-relevant location within 30 ms after saccade offset. This represents the first temporally fine-grained measurement of detection performance in an attention task during the immediate post-saccadic period (0-100 ms), showing that performance recovers to baseline within 30 ms.
evaluation: Claims C2, C8, C13, C29, and C30 converge on the main finding with strong experimental support from Figure 2A showing performance recovery within 30 ms. The statistical analysis using Boschloo's exact test (p>0.1) and adequate trial numbers (at least 48 trials per 10 ms bin from 0-40 ms in Experiment 1) provide rigorous quantitative support. The finding is replicated across two task difficulties in Experiment 2 (C13), ruling out ceiling effects.

result: The rapid post-saccadic recovery time-course resembles that of saccadic suppression recovery, suggesting that retinotopic attentional shifts do not impose additional temporal costs beyond recovery from saccadic suppression.
evaluation: Claims C14, C15, and C31 are supported by comparison with cited previous research on saccadic suppression (Diamond et al., 2000; Dorr and Bex, 2013; McConkie and Loschky, 2002). The similarity in recovery time-courses between the current attention task and previous non-attention tasks provides strong comparative evidence for this inference.

result: Subjects tracked the attentional target veridically throughout the task with extremely low false-positive rates (2.2% and 2% in Experiments 1 and 2), showing no evidence of peri-saccadic spread of attention to irrelevant spatial locations.
evaluation: Claims C3, C9, C21, C22, C23, and C32 are strongly supported by the low false-positive rates across all three experiments. Statistical testing (Boschloo's test, p>0.16) showed no significant increase in false-positives due to retinotopic persistence or predictive shifts. Experiment 3, specifically designed to test these effects with more salient distractor changes, also showed false-positive rates below 1.4%.

result: The recovery time-course after saccades is independent of saccade latency, with similar performance observed for predictive (0-75 ms), express (75-125 ms), and regular-latency (125-250 ms) saccades.
evaluation: Claims C42, C43, and C44 are supported by data shown in Figure 3, which demonstrates very similar performance curves across the three saccade latency groups. This finding is novel and suggests that peri-saccadic attentional shifts proceed with similar time-courses despite potential differences in neural pathways underlying different saccade types.

result: The rapid post-saccadic attentional availability is consistent with physiological data showing attentional effects in monkey V1 emerge approximately 80 ms after saccade offset, and given visual onset latencies of 30-50 ms, changes occurring 30 ms post-saccade would reach visual cortex when neurons are attentionally enhanced.
evaluation: Claims C16 and C17 are supported by citations to relevant physiological studies (Khayat et al., 2004; Bair et al., 2002; Bisley et al., 2004). The inference linking the behavioral findings to neural timing is logically sound given the cited onset latencies, providing cross-species and cross-method convergence.

result: The absence of peri-saccadic attentional spread in this task, unlike previous studies, may reflect differences in task design (single attended location with distractors vs. multiple potential targets) or differential effects of attention on distractor filtering versus signal enhancement.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 present speculative explanations for differences between current and previous findings. While the task design differences are clearly documented (C24, C25), the mechanistic explanations (C26, C27, C28) are explicitly speculative and not directly tested. The authors acknowledge multiple alternative explanations are possible and that extensive additional work would be needed to disambiguate them.

result: Performance was near 100% well before and after saccades, began dropping around fixation point jump time, and dropped steeply immediately before the saccade, consistent with pre-saccadic attentional resource diversion and saccadic suppression.
evaluation: Claims C10, C11, and C12 are directly supported by the performance data in Figure 2A and are consistent with well-established phenomena cited in the literature (Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Diamond et al., 2000; Dorr and Bex, 2013). These findings provide important context for the main result about rapid post-saccadic recovery.

result: Spatial attention and saccadic execution coordinate well to ensure relevant objects are attentionally enhanced soon after the beginning of each eye fixation.
evaluation: Claim C33 is a well-supported inference from the combined findings of rapid performance recovery (C2, C13) and low false-positive rates (C3, C9). The coordination between attention and saccades is demonstrated by the data showing both rapid and accurate attentional allocation post-saccade.

result: Methodological details including subject demographics (10 subjects, 8 in Exp 1, 5 in Exp 2, 4 in Exp 3), task parameters (median RT 324 ms, 90% target changes, 39% distractor changes, 7° saccade), data quality (extremely rare early responses: 1.2%, 1%, 0.7%), and ethical compliance.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41, C45-C47 provide methodological details that are clearly documented and internally consistent. Sample sizes are modest but adequate for the observed effect sizes, with sufficient trials per time bin (at least 48 trials per 10 ms bin in critical periods) for statistical power. Ethical approval is documented.

result: Maintaining attention at a task-relevant location across saccades necessitates rapid, saccade-synchronized shifts of attentional modulation between neuronal populations due to retinotopic visual processing in the brain.
evaluation: Claims C1, C4, and C5 establish the theoretical foundation based on well-established knowledge about retinotopic processing (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Wurtz, 2008; Marino and Mazer, 2016; Yao et al., 2016). These claims provide essential context for understanding why rapid attentional shifts are necessary.

result: Previous research suggested neuronal attention shifts start before and continue after saccades, with evidence for predictive shifts (~75 ms pre-saccade) and retinotopic persistence (up to 100 ms post-saccade), but the precise timing of full attentional allocation remained unclear due to coarse temporal sampling.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C18, C19, and C20 accurately summarize prior literature (Rolfs et al., 2011; Szinte et al., 2015; Golomb et al., 2008, 2010a, 2010b, 2011; Jonikaitis et al., 2013) and identify the gap in knowledge that motivates the current study. The characterization of previous methodological limitations (coarse temporal sampling) is reasonable.
